title: Christmas is a season
hook: the octave and the season run on to the Baptism of the Lord

segments.voice: Yesterday, Advent, four weeks of waiting. Your line was wait well. Did you let a wait in line or in traffic be quiet? Day one hundred forty-five.

December twenty-sixth. The wrapping paper's in the recycling. The radio has abruptly stopped playing carols. By New Year's, trees are lying on the curb, needles everywhere. For most of the culture, Christmas is a single day, and the day after, it's over. But walk into a Catholic church on December twenty-sixth, or on January fifth, and the tree is still lit, the crib is still there, the priest is still in white, and people are still singing Christmas hymns. The party hasn't ended. It's barely started. Today: Christmas is a season.
screen: `DECEMBER 26: TREES ON THE CURB.` → `IN CHURCH, STILL WHITE.` → `THE PARTY HAS BARELY STARTED.`

segments.voice: Christmas, in the Church's calendar, is a season, not a day. It begins on Christmas Eve and runs until the feast of the Baptism of the Lord, in early to mid January. Inside it there are three layers. First, the octave. The Church gives Christmas and Easter an octave: the celebration lasts eight days, as if it's all one long day of joy. The Christmas octave runs from December twenty-fifth to January first, which Catholics keep as the Solemnity of Mary, the Mother of God. Second, the twelve days. That's the old count, from Christmas to the Epiphany on January sixth, the one in the song. Third, the full season, running on to the Baptism of the Lord, when the adult Jesus stands in the Jordan, and the next day Ordinary Time begins. Some families, following an old custom, keep their crib up even longer, until Candlemas on February second. The word Christmas itself is simple: Christ's Mass, from old English. It's named after the Mass. What's the point of a long season? One answer is in Luke. After the shepherds came and went, the Douay-Rheims says: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." She didn't move on. She kept turning it over. The Church asks the same. The feast is too big for one day. So the days after Christmas are full of feasts: Stephen, whom tradition calls the first martyr, John the apostle, the Holy Innocents, the Holy Family. The whole season is a slow pondering of one astonishing claim: God was born.
screen: `A SEASON, NOT A DAY.` · `THE OCTAVE: EIGHT DAYS AS ONE.` · `TWELVE DAYS TO EPIPHANY.` · `ON TO THE BAPTISM OF THE LORD.` · then, large: `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one Christmas thing past the day. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing from Christmas, this past one or the next one, that you could keep going a little longer. A light in the window. A song. A habit of calling someone. A crib on a shelf. Picture it still there in the middle of January. Notice what it would feel like to still be celebrating when everyone else has stopped. If you pray, you can ponder, like Mary, one line of the Christmas story. The bell holds the time.
Christmas is a season. From Christmas Eve through the octave and the twelve days, all the way to the Baptism of the Lord. Today's word.
Your line: Christmas isn't one day. Today, keep one good thing going longer than you normally would: a kindness, a celebration, a thank you. Day one hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Christmas as a season: churches stay decorated and white vestments are worn through the octave and the twelve days until the Baptism of the Lord, and some families leave the tree and crib up until then.

notes: Christmas season ends with the Baptism of the Lord (Sunday after Jan 6, or the Monday after when Epiphany falls on Jan 7 or 8 where it is transferred). Script says 'early to mid January'. Confirm.
Octaves of Christmas and Easter are the only two remaining in the Roman calendar since 1969. Confirm.
Old English Cristes mæsse first recorded c. 1038 (per dictionaries). Original spelled 'Crīstes mæsse' with macron (normalized). Confirm.
Candlemas custom of keeping the crib until February 2: a popular custom. Confirm.
Carry kept exactly as the index ('christmas' lowercase in the carry field; capitalized in the spoken voice).
Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'where Catholics have always celebrated it', the unsourced 'around 1038' and 'only two'; 'first martyr' now attributed to tradition; 'many families' softened.
